source.title: Sketched Ridgeless Linear Regression: The Role of Downsampling
source.authors: Xin Chen; Yicheng Zeng; Siyue Yang; Qiang Sun

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It studies risk curves in ridgeless linear regression, a different model class from deep networks, and reports results bearing on the general double-descent claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own risk curves for linear regression as the aspect ratio varies. It cites deep-network double descent as motivation, but cited results are not recorded. It varies sketching size, not the number of original training samples; it does not measure risk across training epochs. Its optimally sketched curves are included because the text explicitly says their peaks are eliminated.
record.test_reason: In ridgeless linear regression, the paper derives and simulates (n = 400, own code) full-sample risk curves with a peak at p/n = 1 and a second descent (bears on V4). It shows that shrinking the effective sample size m by sketching lowers risk near the threshold (bears on V3). It shows that an optimally chosen sketch size, which the authors frame as regularization, removes the peak (bears on V6). The setting is new (random sketching) but uses a known model class, so T3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that downsampling acts like increasing model capacity ('dual view') and can improve, not only harm, generalization. Orthogonal sketching is optimal in the underparameterized regime, and all sketches are equivalent when overparameterized. Optimally sketched estimators give universally better, stabler risk curves without the full-sample peaks. They attribute the benefit to the non-monotonic risk in aspect ratio, which they note (citing Hastie et al.) disappears under optimally tuned ridge.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes asymptotic and finite-sample risks for ridgeless linear regression, including random sketching; it does not reproduce deep-network size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk curves and peaks vary with whether sketching is used and with sketching type; the paper also reports curves under differing SNR and feature covariance settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Central limit theorems show that optimally sketched estimators can have smaller asymptotic risk variance than full-sample estimators.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near the interpolation threshold, the variability of test risk (not only its mean) can be reduced by moving away from the threshold.

record.problems: Evidence concerns ridgeless linear regression rather than deep networks. The numerical risk curves use n = 400, and plotted finite-sample results are not tabulated. The paper does not test epoch-wise behavior or increasing the original training-sample count.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results were left out. Results about computational runtime, validation-set selection, and CLTs were not included because they do not separately measure a claim version's risk-curve behavior.

untested.parts: All: no deep networks or model-size sweeps of neural nets.
All: no training-time or epoch axis; the estimators are closed-form.
Deep networks, and adding genuinely new samples. Only effective sample size via sketching is varied, in linear regression.
All: no unified effective-complexity measure across size, epochs and samples is proposed. The p/m aspect ratio unifies only size and samples within linear regression.

Label noise as a driver is not studied empirically; the σ² term in the formula is only implicit. Multiple or triple peaks are not examined. Optimally tuned ridge is only cited from Hastie et al., not tested.
Model classes other than linear least squares; random-feature and kernel models are only mentioned as future work.

missing.what: Limiting risk as a function of downsampling ratio ψ = m/n. Risk is non-monotone in effective sample size, and the optimal m* = (α−σ)p/α < n when SNR > 1 and ϕ is near 1, i.e. fewer samples lower risk.
missing.locator: Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3, Figure 2 (n = 400, p = 200, SNR 1 and 3); Figure 4 (correlated); Figure 7 (m* = 247 for p = 424)

missing.what: Sketch size chosen empirically on a validation set (n_val = 20, 100, 200) also yields stable, monotone risk curves without the peak, close to the m* curve.
Elimination of the peak at low SNR (0.75), where the optimal choice is the null estimator m* = 0 for large ϕ.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 limits_scope label on R2/R4/R5 is moved: an optimally tuned estimator removing the peak is what V6 predicts, not a scope limit on V4. The reader marked V3 as untested because sketching is not adding original samples. However, orthogonal sketching makes the risk depend on p/m exactly as if m samples were used, and the authors frame it as reducing sample size, so V3 is credited for linear regression only. The full-sample formula is from Hastie et al.; only the Figure 1 simulations are the study's own. Misspecified-model results (Section 6.3) are not linked to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error across model sizes.
Risk as the number of original training samples increases near interpolation; changing sketching size is not that measurement.
The paper tests ridgeless linear regression, not every model class; its results do not establish the generality of the curve across model classes.
A unified effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.

Whether noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak. The paper mentions tuned ridge results from other work but does not test them.
Whether counting effective parameters converts second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: full-sample ridgeless least square estimator
rows.size_stated: p features; n samples; both tend to infinity proportionally
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed asymptotic out-of-sample risk as the aspect ratio ϕ = p/n varies.

conditions.value: general α and σ; SNR = α/σ

rows.value: For ϕ < 1: σ²ϕ/(1−ϕ). For ϕ > 1: α²(1−ϕ⁻¹) + σ²/(ϕ−1).
rows.uncertainty: Almost-sure limiting result; central limit results are also given elsewhere in the paper.
rows.locator: Section 3.1, full-sample risk formula following Theorem 3.2; Figure 1
rows.note: The stated risk curve diverges at the interpolation ratio and decreases again in the overparameterized regime.
rows.check: The formula is a stated variant of Hastie et al. (2022) Theorem 1, a cited result. The paper's own evidence is the Figure 1 finite-sample simulations (n = 400; SNR 1, 2, 3 with (α,σ) = (5,5), (10,5), (15,5)). The conditions should say this rather than 'general α and σ'.

rows.subject: orthogonally sketched ridgeless least square estimator with optimal sketching size m*
rows.size_stated: n = 400 in the finite-sample plot; p varies with ϕ
rows.operation_detail: Varied ϕ and selected the sketching size using the theoretical optimum described in Theorem 3.3.
rows.value: The optimally sketched risk curve eliminates the peaks observed for the full-sample estimator.
rows.note: The curve is plotted against ϕ, with m* selected based on SNR and ϕ.
rows.check: Re-link from V4 to V6. Removing the peak with an optimally tuned estimator is what V6 names; it is not a failure of the full-sample double-descent curve that V4 describes. As a V6 result the state is observed. Caveat: the tuning is of sketch size, not ridge, though the authors call downsampling a form of regularization. Figure 3 also has a left panel (SNR = 0.75) with the same elimination, which the row omits.
